methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a prospective single-arm, open-label phase II cohort within a multicohort platform trial with a prespecified primary endpoint (IRC-assessed ORR at TMB ≥16 mut/Mb) benchmarked against a 10% standard-of-care threshold, with IRC central review providing blinded response adjudication. Clopper–Pearson CIs for ORR and Kaplan–Meier estimation for DOR/PFS/OS are appropriate for the data types, and the efficacy- and safety-evaluable populations are defined. Key weaknesses: no randomized comparator, no formal sample-size justification or power calculation is reported, there is no multiplicity correction across the many secondary/subgroup/assay analyses (FMI tissue, non-FMI local, FMI blood, TPS/CPS, tumor-type subsets), and interpretation of across-assay differences is complicated by overlapping populations and small subgroups (e.g., n=20 for TPS ≥1%). Missing data handling and censoring beyond the time-to-CNS-progression rule are not fully detailed. Limitations (variability of TMB assays, MSI not analyzed, CNS inclusion) are explicitly acknowledged in the Discussion.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is a single-arm, open-label prospective phase II cohort (TAPISTRY cohort D) comparing ORR to a historical/standard-of-care benchmark; by Oxford CEBM 2011 this maps to 2b (individual cohort / low-quality trial without randomization). Clinical relevance is moderate: the question (whether atezolizumab benefits TMB-high solid tumors and which TMB cutoff is informative) is important given pembrolizumab's tumor-agnostic approval at ≥10 mut/Mb, and the trial provides prospective data at two cutoffs across diverse tumor types including pediatric eligibility. However, the ORR of 22.3% (≥16) and 20.2% (≥13) is only moderate, DOR is not estimable, PFS is short (~2.7–2.8 months), and findings are unlikely to be practice-changing or support a tumor-agnostic label for atezolizumab, limiting direct clinical impact beyond informing biomarker/cutoff strategy.

reporting_quality.justification: CONSORT (adapted for non-randomized single-arm trials) is the applicable standard. Strengths include trial registration (NCT04589845), prespecified primary endpoint and threshold, clear eligibility criteria, defined analysis populations, central IRC adjudication, detailed AE classification (CTCAE v5.0, SAE definitions), and a patient-flow figure. Gaps include absent sample-size/power justification, no explicit CONSORT checklist, limited reporting of protocol amendments, and heavy reliance on supplementary tables for AE detail and representativeness. Data/code availability is weak: no mention of raw data deposition, analysis code sharing, or participant-level data access; the manuscript states SAS v9.4 was used but provides no code or repository identifier, warranting a low availability score even allowing for blinded redactions.

novelty_literature.justification: The study is an empirical extension of prior work (Legrand 2018; Gandara 2018; B-F1RST; MyPathway) confirming that atezolizumab has activity in TMB-high solid tumors at ≥13 and ≥16 mut/Mb cutoffs. The prospective, tumor-agnostic design with head-to-head comparison of FMI tissue, FMI blood, and non-FMI local assays within a single cohort adds incremental methodological value, but the mechanism, drug, biomarker, and cutoffs have all been studied previously (notably KEYNOTE-158 for pembrolizumab and multiple retrospective atezolizumab analyses). The paper does not establish a new biomarker, mechanism, or paradigm; it confirms moderate activity without defining a superior cutoff, which the authors themselves describe as 'moderate antitumor activity.'

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written and logically organized: the Introduction frames the TMB-cutoff heterogeneity problem, Methods are detailed on eligibility, assays, and endpoints, and Results are structured by assay and cutoff. The abstract is quantitatively grounded and accurately reflects the body (ORR, CIs, PFS, AE rates). Table and figure captions are informative and standalone-interpretable (e.g., Fig 1 flow, Fig 2 KM plots). Minor weaknesses include dense parenthetical reporting of multiple assay subgroup statistics that could benefit from a consolidated results figure, and some repetition between Results and Discussion of the FMI-tissue vs blood comparison.

key_strengths: Prospective, tumor-agnostic phase II platform cohort with prespecified primary endpoint (IRC-assessed ORR at TMB ≥16 mut/Mb) benchmarked against a 10% standard-of-care threshold
Central IRC adjudication and standardized RECIST v1.1 assessment reduce response-ascertainment bias
Direct comparison of FMI tissue, FMI blood, and non-FMI local TMB assays within the same cohort informs biomarker/cutoff debate
Safety reporting is thorough with CTCAE v5.0 grading, SAE definitions, AEs of special interest, and no new signals
Transparent discussion of limitations including MSI not analyzed, CNS inclusion, small subgroups, and pediatric under-enrollment
key_concerns: Single-arm design with historical 10% comparator limits causal inference; no randomized control
No reported sample-size/power justification and no multiplicity correction across many assay- and PD-L1-based subgroup analyses
Clinical activity is moderate (ORR 22.3% at ≥16, 20.2% at ≥13; median PFS ~2.7–2.8 months) and unlikely to be practice-changing or support a tumor-agnostic label
Novelty is largely confirmatory of prior retrospective atezolizumab TMB analyses and KEYNOTE-158-era findings; no definitive cutoff selected
Data/code availability is not addressed; no repository or analysis-code identifier provided
Small per-tumor and per-PD-L1-subgroup Ns (e.g., TPS ≥1% n=20) make the exploratory findings hypothesis-generating only
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competently conducted prospective phase II platform cohort with modest but credible activity, appropriate statistics for a single-arm design, and transparent limitations; novelty and clinical impact are incremental, placing it comfortably in tier 2 (mid-tier oncology journals) with minor revisions to strengthen multiplicity handling and data-availability reporting.
